name: Groundwork Data Center Site Diligence Checklist
note: Framework checklist for data center site acquisition diligence. Each item needs jurisdiction-specific verification by counsel before reliance.

workstreams.title: Power & Utility
workstreams.intro: Power is the deal. A site without a credible megawatt story is a farm field with a nice survey. This workstream usually decides go/no-go before anything else is worth spending money on.

items.item: Identify the serving utility and confirm exclusive service territory
items.why: Territory disputes and unclear service rights between an IOU, a co-op, or a municipal utility can add years. In some states territory is contestable; in others it is fixed by statute or commission order.
items.red_flags: Site straddles two service territories; co-op territory with limited large-load experience; municipal utility with no transmission-level interconnection history.

items.item: Obtain a will-serve or load study commitment in writing, with capacity and timeline
items.why: Verbal 'we can serve you' means nothing. The letter should state MW available, voltage, delivery point, required system upgrades, and an estimated energization schedule.
items.red_flags: Utility will only commit to 'study queue' status; energization date beyond 4-5 years; capacity conditioned on unbuilt generation or transmission.

items.item: Review the utility's large-load tariff and any pending large-load rate cases
items.why: Multiple states have adopted or proposed special data center tariffs: minimum take-or-pay terms, long contract tenors (10-15 yrs), collateral requirements, and exit fees. These reshape project economics and financeability.
items.red_flags: Pending rate case that could impose retroactive terms; take-or-pay minimums above realistic ramp; termination fees that survive assignment.

items.item: Map distance to existing transmission and substation capacity
items.why: A new 230kV+ substation and transmission tap is a multi-year, $50M+ undertaking with its own siting, NEPA/state-EIS, and condemnation risks. Proximity to existing headroom is worth a premium on land price.
items.red_flags: Nearest transmission line >5 miles; substation expansion requires new right-of-way through residential or environmentally sensitive land.

items.item: Assess interconnection queue position and regional (RTO/ISO) constraints
items.why: In constrained RTO regions, queue position is an asset that conveys (or doesn't) with the land. Confirm whether any queue rights exist, who holds them, and whether they are assignable.
items.red_flags: Seller markets 'power available' based on a queue position held by an affiliate that doesn't convey; cluster-study restart risk.

items.item: Evaluate behind-the-meter / on-site generation options and their regulatory posture
items.why: Gas turbines, fuel cells, and bridging generation can rescue a timeline, but several states are moving to regulate or surcharge behind-the-meter large loads. Air permits for on-site generation are their own critical path.
items.red_flags: Nonattainment area for NOx/ozone making air permits slow; state legislation pending on BTM large-load cost allocation.

items.item: Confirm who pays for system upgrades and on what schedule (CIAC exposure)
items.why: Contribution-in-aid-of-construction obligations can run nine figures and are often due before financing milestones. Tax treatment of CIAC matters too.
items.red_flags: Open-ended upgrade cost true-up clauses; utility requires full prepayment with no refund mechanism if capacity is later shared.

items.item: Review curtailment, demand-response, and non-firm service terms
items.why: Some fast-track interconnection products are conditioned on curtailability. Acceptable for some tenants, fatal for others — know the end user before accepting non-firm terms.
items.red_flags: Unlimited curtailment hours; curtailment triggers defined solely at utility discretion.

workstreams.title: Land Use, Zoning & Entitlements
workstreams.intro: The entitlement climate for data centers shifted hard after 2023. By-right today is not by-right at closing unless you protect it. This is where a CRE lawyer earns the fee.

items.item: Confirm current zoning permits data center use by right, by special exception, or not at all
items.why: Many jurisdictions have re-classified data centers out of by-right industrial categories or added special-exception requirements with discretionary review.
items.red_flags: Use is permitted only via legislative rezoning; pending zoning ordinance amendment targeting data centers; 'data center' undefined in the code (interpretation risk).

items.item: Check for pending or threatened moratoria at county, city, and town level
items.why: Data center moratoria have been adopted with little warning in multiple states. A moratorium between PSA signing and entitlement vesting can strand a deposit.
items.red_flags: Council member statements or citizen petitions advocating a pause; comprehensive plan update in progress that revisits data center policy.

items.item: Determine when development rights vest under state law and structure the PSA around it
items.why: Vesting rules vary enormously: some states vest at complete application, others only at building permit. The PSA's diligence and closing conditions should track the actual vesting trigger.
items.red_flags: Long gap between closing obligation and vesting event; jurisdiction with history of downzoning during application pendency.

items.item: Review setback, height, noise, and screening standards specific to data centers
items.why: Newer ordinances impose data-center-specific noise limits (often dBA at property line), generator setbacks, and substation screening that can cut buildable envelope materially.
items.red_flags: Noise standard measured at residential property line with homes <500 ft; generator yard orientation constrained by adjacency.

items.item: Identify all discretionary approvals and their realistic timelines (rezoning, SUP, site plan, comp plan amendment)
items.why: Each discretionary step is a public hearing, which is an organizing opportunity for opposition. Map the full approval stack and the political calendar (elections matter).
items.red_flags: Approval requires supermajority after protest petition; hearing schedule pushes decision past an election with anti-data-center candidates.

items.item: Check proffer / development agreement / community benefit expectations
items.why: In competitive jurisdictions, road improvements, fiscal contributions, and design proffers are the de facto price of approval. Budget them like hard costs.
items.red_flags: Recent comparable approvals carried proffers materially above your pro forma; jurisdiction has no development agreement statute (handshake risk).

workstreams.title: Water, Sewer & Cooling
workstreams.intro: Cooling technology choices drive water demand, and water is the most politically combustible input after power — especially in the West.

items.item: Quantify water demand under the actual cooling design (evaporative vs. closed-loop vs. air-cooled) and confirm supply
items.why: Demand ranges from near-zero (air-cooled) to millions of gallons/day (evaporative). Get the will-serve from the water purveyor sized to the real design, with peak-day numbers.
items.red_flags: Purveyor capacity letter caps supply below peak design day; supply contingent on unbuilt treatment capacity.

items.item: Confirm water rights regime and whether new appropriations are realistically available
items.why: In prior-appropriation states, municipal supply may be the only practical path; new rights can be effectively unobtainable. Groundwater management areas add another layer.
items.red_flags: Site in a groundwater management/active management area with moratorium on new wells; water rights marketed with the land are unadjudicated or relinquishment-prone.

items.item: Review sewer/industrial discharge capacity and pretreatment requirements for blowdown
items.why: Cooling tower blowdown is an industrial discharge. POTW capacity and pretreatment permits are routinely overlooked until design development.
items.red_flags: POTW at or near permitted capacity; TDS limits that force on-site treatment.

items.item: Assess reclaimed/recycled water availability as both cost saver and political mitigation
items.why: Purple-pipe supply materially de-risks the public narrative and may be cheaper. Some jurisdictions now effectively require it for large users.
items.red_flags: Reclaimed main >3 miles away with no extension plan; reclaimed supply already fully subscribed.

items.item: Phase I ESA (and Phase II if RECs) under current ASTM standard, with non-scope items considered
items.why: Baseline CERCLA innocent-landowner protection. For data centers, also ask the consultant to address PFAS (firefighting systems history) and historic agricultural chemical use.
items.red_flags: Former industrial/landfill/orchard use; dry cleaner or UST history on or adjacent; vapor pathways near planned office space.

items.item: Wetlands/waters delineation and 404/401 permitting exposure
items.why: Large-pad grading on greenfield sites frequently touches jurisdictional waters; mitigation banking costs and Corps timelines belong in the schedule and budget.
items.red_flags: Mapped streams/wetlands across the buildable area; recent jurisdictional rule changes in flux for the region.

items.item: Threatened/endangered species and critical habitat screening
items.why: A listed species survey window can freeze grading for a season. Know the survey calendar before signing a construction-start commitment.
items.red_flags: Site in mapped critical habitat; survey windows that don't align with the construction schedule.

items.item: Air permitting pathway for backup generators (and any bridging generation)
items.why: A 100+ MW campus can carry dozens of 2-3 MW diesel generators — minor source vs. major source determination drives a 6-24 month spread in timeline.
items.red_flags: Nonattainment designation; aggregation risk with neighboring facilities under common control.

items.item: Stormwater, floodplain, and geotech screening
items.why: Data halls are flat, heavy, and water-averse. FEMA floodplain on the pad or poor soils (expansive clay, shallow rock, high groundwater) move real money.
items.red_flags: Any floodway touch; karst terrain; groundwater within excavation depth of mission-critical vaults.

workstreams.title: Title, Survey & Land
workstreams.intro: Standard CRE title work, but with data-center-specific traps: easement corridors, mineral severance under big pads, and assemblage seams.

items.item: Full title commitment review with data-center lens on easements and use restrictions
items.why: Pipeline, transmission, and fiber easements crossing the pad area are not minor exceptions here — they dictate building placement. CC&Rs with use or height restrictions can quietly prohibit the project.
items.red_flags: Blanket easements without defined location; private restrictions requiring third-party consent for industrial use; reversionary clauses tied to use.

items.item: Mineral estate severance and surface-use risk
items.why: In severed-estate states, the mineral owner's implied right of reasonable surface use is incompatible with a mission-critical facility. Surface waivers or accommodation agreements may be needed.
items.red_flags: Active leases or recent mineral conveyances; state with strong mineral-dominance doctrine; no surface waiver obtainable.

items.item: ALTA survey with utility corridor, easement, and encroachment mapping against the conceptual site plan
items.why: Overlay the survey on the power and fiber routing plan early — the cheapest time to discover a corridor conflict is before the deposit goes hard.
items.red_flags: Gaps or gores in an assemblage; boundary line agreements needed with multiple neighbors.

items.item: Assemblage strategy: option structure, confidentiality, and holdout exposure
items.why: Multi-parcel campuses live or die on sequencing. Options with staged exercise, name-shielded entities, and uniform pricing discipline prevent the last parcel from costing more than the first ten.
items.red_flags: Key center parcel not yet under control; broker leakage of end-user identity; recorded memoranda tipping the market.

items.item: Existing agricultural/forestry tax classification and rollback/penalty exposure on conversion
items.why: Current-use programs (ag deferral, forestland classification) trigger rollback taxes and penalties on change of use — a real number on 200+ acre sites, and allocation between buyer/seller belongs in the PSA.
items.red_flags: Decade-plus of deferral accumulated; statute imposes penalty in addition to rollback; PSA silent on allocation.

items.item: State sales/use tax exemption for data center equipment: eligibility thresholds, sunset dates, and clawbacks
items.why: Equipment is 70-80% of project cost and refreshes every 4-6 years; the sales tax exemption is usually the single largest incentive. Eligibility thresholds (investment, jobs, wages) and certification timing are strict.
items.red_flags: Program sunset before refresh cycles; pending legislation to repeal or condition the exemption; jobs covenant the operating model can't meet.

items.item: Property tax treatment of real vs. personal property, and abatement availability
items.why: Classification of servers, generators, and electrical gear as real vs. personal property varies by state and drives the assessed base. Local abatements (PILOT, FILOT, Chapter-style agreements) are negotiable instruments — paper them like contracts.
items.red_flags: County reassessment cycle landing mid-construction; abatement requires annual reapplication; assessor history of aggressive 'fixtures' positions.

items.item: Negotiated incentive agreements: performance covenants, clawbacks, transferability
items.why: Incentive agreements are contracts with default provisions. Confirm they survive an asset sale or REIT transfer, and model the clawback as a contingent liability.
items.red_flags: Non-assignable incentives in a build-to-sell strategy; clawback triggered by headcount metrics outside operator control.

items.item: Transfer tax / recording cost structuring on acquisition (entity vs. asset, applicable exemptions)
items.why: On nine-figure land deals, real estate excise/transfer tax planning is real money. Controlling-interest transfer rules catch entity deals in several states.
items.red_flags: State with controlling-interest transfer tax and lookback period; county-level surcharge recently enacted.

items.item: Utility tax, gross receipts tax, and franchise fee exposure on power purchases
items.why: A facility buying $100M+/yr of electricity cares about every percentage point of utility tax. Some municipalities tax utility sales at 5-6%; site selection inside vs. outside city limits can be an eight-figure NPV decision.
items.red_flags: Annexation risk into a high-utility-tax city; gross receipts tax regimes reaching colocation revenue.

items.item: Identify long-haul and metro fiber routes serving the site and distance to splice points
items.why: Two diverse fiber paths is the standard. Lit buildings nearby help, but what matters is conduit rights and construction cost to reach diverse backbone routes.
items.red_flags: Single fiber corridor serving the area; railroad or limited-access highway crossing required for diversity.

items.item: Confirm rights-of-way and franchise/permit pathway for new fiber laterals
items.why: Fiber laterals cross public ROW and private land; county franchise requirements and railroad crossing agreements have their own timelines (railroads are famously slow).
items.red_flags: Railroad crossing on every diverse-path option; private easements needed from uncooperative neighbors.

items.item: Latency profile to relevant exchange points / availability zones
items.why: For some workloads proximity to existing cloud regions or IXPs is a leasing prerequisite; for AI training it matters less. Know the target tenant before pricing this in.
items.red_flags: Marketing the site for latency-sensitive use at distances the physics doesn't support.

workstreams.title: Community, Political & Legal Risk
workstreams.intro: Data centers have become a local political issue in a way warehouses never were. Quiet sites get loud fast.

items.item: Map the opposition landscape: organized groups, recent contested projects, local press tone
items.why: A jurisdiction's last data center fight predicts your hearing. Search local coverage, planning commission minutes, and citizen group activity before relying on a 'business friendly' label.
items.red_flags: Active anti-data-center citizen group; prior project withdrawn or denied; moratorium adopted in an adjacent jurisdiction (contagion).

items.item: Review pending state legislation touching data centers (tariffs, incentives, siting, water, noise)
items.why: Legislative sessions have produced large-load tariff mandates, incentive repeals, and siting bills with short fuses. A pending bill can change the deal between LOI and closing.
items.red_flags: Bill with momentum that conditions incentives on ratepayer protections your pro forma didn't assume.

items.item: Check for litigation risk patterns: land use appeals, NEPA/state-EIS challenges, ratepayer complaints
items.why: Serial land-use appellants and well-funded environmental petitioners can add 12-24 months even when they lose. Price the delay, not just the merits.
items.red_flags: State with liberal land-use standing rules and a history of data center appeals; utility's certificate proceedings already contested.

items.item: Election calendar and key-decision-maker mapping
items.why: Approvals that span an election are hostage to it. Know which seats turn over before your hearing dates and what the candidates are saying about data centers.
items.red_flags: Project approval scheduled within 90 days of a contested local election where the project is an issue.
